segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore you are without excuse, whoever you are, you who judge. For in judging the other person you condemn yourself, because you who judge practice the very same things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we know that God’s judgment on those who practice such things accords with truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do you suppose, whoever you are, you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness is leading you toward turning back?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But because of your hardness and your heart that refuses to turn back, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who will repay each person according to their works:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but for those who act out of selfish ambition and disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There will be affliction and distress for every human being who does what is evil, the Jew first and also the Greek,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does what is good, the Jew first and also the Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there is no partiality with God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous in God’s sight; it is the doers of the law who will be justified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whenever Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, these, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They show that the work of the law is written in their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their thoughts among themselves accuse or even excuse them

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: on the day when God judges what is hidden in people, according to my good news, through Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and know his will and discern what matters most, being instructed from the law,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and are confident that you yourself are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of little children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: you, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who detest idols, do you rob temples?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by transgressing the law?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, just as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For circumcision is of benefit if you practice the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if an uncircumcised man keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the one who is uncircumcised by nature yet fulfills the law will judge you, who have the letter and circumcision and yet are a transgressor of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a person is not a Jew by what is visible, nor is circumcision what is visible in the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rather, a person is a Jew by what is hidden, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter. Such a person’s praise comes not from people but from God.

notes.note: The Greek is a brusque vocative, literally “O person,” common in the lively question-and-answer style of ancient moral teachers, where the speaker argues with an imagined individual. “O man” is the traditional rendering, but it is archaic and sounds gender-specific where the Greek is not. The singular “you” throughout this chapter addresses that imagined partner, not a named individual; who he represents in verses 1–16 (a moralizing Gentile, a Jew, or anyone who judges) is debated.

Most translations keep “repentance,” understood as including a change of life. In modern English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in Jewish usage carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. The related adjective in verse 5 is rendered “that refuses to turn back” (traditionally “impenitent” or “unrepentant”).

notes.phrase: who will repay each person according to their works
notes.note: Paul’s wording closely follows the Greek version of Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, though he does not mark it as a quotation. His first readers who knew the Scriptures would have recognized a settled principle of Jewish belief about God’s judgment.

The word is rare before the New Testament; its earlier use, in Aristotle, concerns the self-interested pursuit of political office. Older versions linked it with a similar-sounding word for “strife” and translated “contentious,” but most scholars now prefer “selfish ambition” or “self-seeking.” The exact nuance remains uncertain.

“Righteous” and “justified” here, “just judgment” in verse 5, “unrighteousness” in verse 8 and “righteous requirements” in verse 26 all belong to one Greek word-family, where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). To be “justified” is to be declared in the right. How this statement that doers of the law will be justified fits with Paul’s later argument (3:20) is much discussed; some take it as hypothetical, others as a real description of the final judgment.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. The same word is translated “nations” elsewhere when peoples as ethnic or political units are in view.

The phrase can be attached to what follows (Gentiles “do by nature what the law requires”) or to what precedes (Gentiles “who do not have the law by nature,” that is, by birth). Most translations take the first option, as here. A number of scholars prefer the second, noting the similar expression “uncircumcised by nature” in verse 27, and some of them think Paul has Gentile Christians in view.

notes.phrase: on the day when God judges
notes.traditional: in the day when God shall judge
notes.note: The link with verse 15 is abrupt, and some interpreters treat verses 14–15 as a parenthesis so that this verse continues verse 13 (“will be justified … on the day”). The verb can be read as present (“judges”) or future (“will judge”); the two differ only by an accent, which the earliest manuscripts did not write. Either way the final judgment is meant.

“Gospel” is the traditional rendering and many modern translations alternate between the two. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations, whereas “gospel” now sounds like a purely religious term or a book title.

notes.traditional: dost thou commit sacrilege; do you rob temples
notes.note: The verb literally means to plunder a temple, and it also had a wider sense of committing sacrilege. Paul may mean actual theft or profit from goods taken from pagan shrines, which the Law forbade (Deuteronomy 7:25), or more loosely any irreverent treatment of what is sacred, perhaps even withholding what was owed to the Jerusalem temple. The precise reference is uncertain.

notes.phrase: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”
notes.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 52:5 in the Greek version, which includes “because of you” and “among the Gentiles”; the Hebrew text is shorter. In Greek, “just as it is written” stands at the end of the sentence, an unusual position; it is moved forward here for English.

notes.phrase: by the Spirit, not the letter
notes.traditional: in the spirit, and not in the letter
notes.note: The Greek can mean “in spirit,” an inward as opposed to a literal circumcision, or “by the Spirit,” God’s Spirit as the one who brings it about. Many scholars favor the second in light of Paul’s similar contrast of Spirit and letter in Romans 7:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, but the first is also widely held. “Letter” means what is written, here the law as a written code.

Many interpreters hear a wordplay here: “Jew” derives from “Judah,” a name that Genesis 29:35 and 49:8 connect with the Hebrew verb “to praise.” The pun works in Hebrew and not in Greek, so it is uncertain whether Paul intended it or expected readers in Rome to catch it.

candidates.reason: Paul uses it with and without the article for the Mosaic law, a principle, or Scripture, and translators differ on capitalization and on whether to supply “the”; consistency across Romans and Galatians matters.
It is the negative of the δικαιοσύνη family, and versions vary between unrighteousness, injustice, wickedness and wrongdoing, which hides the link to “righteousness.”
The accounting sense (count, reckon, credit) is central to Romans 4 and Galatians 3 and needs one fixed English verb.
It recurs throughout Paul in both good and bad senses, and versions vary between boast, glory, rejoice and take pride.
Versions split between endurance, perseverance, patience and steadfastness across Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation.
